judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 1 Skills about accumulating word knowledge, but in different skill areas and sub-strands: the first is Term 2 Writing / Shared, Group and Independent Writing ('Begins to build own word bank and personal dictionary using initial letter of words such as ant, book, cat'), the second is Term 3 Reading and Phonics / Group Guided Reading ('Continues to build a sight vocabulary from the incidental reading programme, the graded reading series and high-frequency word lists'). Shared LC tag 'vocabulary' and shared wording are limited to 'build ... word', and the mechanisms differ (alphabetic organisation of a personal written word bank by initial letter versus automatic whole-word recognition drawn from graded reading and high-frequency lists). The second statement's 'Continues to build' signals an ongoing reading-programme strand rather than dependence on the writing word bank, so the evidence supports meaningful complementary word-knowledge coherence across reading and writing but not a developmental dependency, even though the Term 2 to Term 3 order would permit first_to_second. Endpoint source evidence and the second endpoint's LC metadata are truncated, which further limits support for asserting a directional progression.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 3, Term 3 Skill bullets under the same Sub-strand 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' (Writing skill area), printed in the same table row/page. One concerns composing with varied sentence types (statements, questions, commands); the other concerns reading one's own written text aloud to the class. These are complementary components of the same independent-writing cycle (compose, then share/present own writing) and mutually reinforce authorship, but neither statement's evidence shows that proficiency in one is needed for or substantively develops into the other, and both sit at the same grade and term rank with no expanded-capability contrast. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment; the shared ancestry and the single shared token 'writing' alone would not justify a developmental direction. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and carries upstream merge/audit context, so absence of further qualifying text is not proof of absence.

This is a cross-skill-area oral-to-reading comprehension support, not generic repetition. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and ancestors carry merge/audit context (Grade and Term banner nodes merged across skill areas), so the judgment rests on the supplied statement text, Term/Skill Area scope and Learning Components only.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R emergent-literacy Skills grounded in pretend/role-play behaviour: 'Role-plays writing in play situations: takes a telephone message, writes a traffic fine etc.' (Term 1, Skill Area EMERGENT WRITING, Sub-strand Emergent Writing) and 'Pretends to ‘read’ and adopts a ‘reading’ voice' (Term 3, Skill Area EMERGENT READING, Sub-strand Emergent reading skills). Their LC tags overlap on 'pretend'/'emergent' (pretend writing vs pretend reading), showing genuine conceptual coherence in simulating literate behaviour during play. However, they sit in different skill areas and neither statement extends, deepens, or depends on the other: role-playing the act of writing a message is not evidence-backed support for adopting a reading voice with books, and the shared Grade R coordinate plus weak token/trigram overlap (jaccard ~0.05) alone cannot establish developmental direction despite the admissible Term 1 → Term 3 order. Symmetric relatesTo captures the complementary reinforcement without asserting dependency. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so unseen source detail could refine but does not currently support a developmental claim.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs carry the identical CAPS statement 'Monitors self when reading, both word recognition and comprehension' and the same Learning Component (a4efed48), and both sit under the Group Guided Reading sub-strand of Reading and Phonics in Term 4. The source refs show different grade scopes: Grade 1 / Term 4 (rank 1, window 24) and Grade 2 / Term 4 (rank 2, window 38), so direction is lower-to-higher rank only. This is more than generic repetition: the Grade 2 occurrence sits in a Group Guided Reading row that also lists self-correcting strategies (re-reading, pausing, practising a word before saying it aloud) applied to the more demanding Grade 2 guided-reading texts, so the same self-monitoring behaviour is exercised over longer, harder text with greater independence. Establishing self-monitoring of word recognition and comprehension in Grade 1 guided reading supports success with the Grade 2 expectation, so buildsTowards from the Grade 1 skill to the Grade 2 skill is justified. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence and supporting LC evidence are truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each), so the full Grade 2 elaboration is not visible in this bounded excerpt; this lowers confidence but the visible grade coordinates, sub-strand placement and row context are consistent.

Same-grade/same-term direction is permitted (Term 2 to Term 2) and is justified by this substantive foundational-to-applied relationship rather than by shared ancestors or token overlap. Direction therefore runs from the Term 1 node (second) to the Term 4 node (first), consistent with earlier-to-later term ordering within one grade. Shared Grade ancestor and the 'phonics' LC tag alone were not treated as sufficient; the judgment rests on the statement texts. Term 2 to Term 3 would be a permitted forward direction, but the developmental claim is not supported, so the symmetric relation is the defensible judgment. judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade 3 (rank 3) Skills under Reading and Phonics / 'Phonic Activities three times a week for 15 minutes:' (canonical Phonics): the first (Term 2) is 'Uses words in written sentences that are pronounced the same way, but have different meanings' (read/reed); the second (Term 3) is 'Recognises silent letters in words' (k in know, l in half, b in comb, w in write, h in hour). They share substantive, pair-specific coherence as word-level phonics skills dealing with non-transparent spelling-sound relationships in consecutive terms of the same sub-strand, so each meaningfully reinforces the other. However, they are parallel, distinct phonic phenomena: the Term 3 statement does not expand, combine, or increase the complexity of homophone use, and no evidence shows that homophone proficiency supports success in recognising silent letters, so a developmental buildsTowards is not warranted. Nomination support is weak (rank_gap 0 'weak' local proximity; SFI/LC text Jaccard 0.07 driven by 'in', 'that', 'words'; LC tag overlap only on generic 'phonics' and 'word', with distinct specific tags homophones/word meaning versus silent letters/word recognition). relatesTo is symmetric with null direction and canonical endpoint order preserved. Evidence is bounded: 24 source-evidence items omitted per endpoint and merged Grade/Term banner ancestry, so confidence is moderate.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs sit in Grade 2 (rank 2) but in different skill areas and terms: the first is Term 4 Listening and Speaking (Oral), 'Listens to a complex sequence of instructions and responds appropriately' (sub-strand: Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities); the second is Term 1 Reading and Phonics / Shared Reading, 'Reads simple instructions in the classroom'. Their shared substance is comprehending and acting on classroom instructions, evidenced by the common LC tag/token 'instructions' and the parallel LC descriptions, so they are mutually reinforcing complementary modalities (oral comprehension vs decoding simple written classroom text). However, the oral target is not developmentally dependent on reading simple written instructions, and the two are governed by different sub-strands and sequencing (written-text decoding is a reading-strand progression, not a precondition for responding to spoken instruction sequences); likewise a Term 4 oral statement cannot build towards a Term 1 statement within the same grade. Conceptual coherence without dependency supports a symmetric relatesTo. Note both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and all endpoints/ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R (rank 0) Listening and Speaking (Oral) Skills using puzzle activities: the first is Term 2 'Solves and completes ten or more piece jig-saw puzzles' under the sub-strand 'Uses language to investigate and explore'; the second is Term 4 'Matches pictures and words using puzzles' under 'Uses visual and pictorial cues to make meaning'. The shared evidence is the puzzle medium and visual discrimination/matching work (LC tags 'puzzles' overlap; sfi/LC token overlap limited to 'and'/'puzzles'), giving genuine conceptual coherence in hands-on visual meaning-making. However, the Term 4 statement's distinctive demand is associating printed words with pictures, an emergent-print capability that jig-saw completion (spatial part-whole problem solving under a different sub-strand) does not specifically support, so the evidence does not justify an asserted Term 2 to Term 4 developmental dependency. Reinforcement/complementarity is supported, dependency is not. Note both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all supplied nodes carry upstream audit/merge context, so judgment rests on the bounded printed statements, identity scopes and LC metadata shown.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills are Grade R (resolved coordinates, rank 0). The second (Term 1, Listening and Speaking (Oral), 'Recites simple rhymes and does actions (with help)'; LCs tagged actions/movement/rhymes and oral/reciting/rhymes) is memorised oral recitation with accompanying physical actions. The first (Term 2, Emergent Reading / Shared Reading, 'Responds to stories through movement and drama activities or rings'; LC tagged drama/movement/responding/stories) is a comprehension-level response to a shared narrative enacted through movement and drama. These are complementary Grade R enactment practices: both use physical/dramatic response to an oral text, and both source contexts anchor the activity in the Grade R 'rings' (the Term 1 row describes activities introduced during the Grade R rings; the Term 2 statement names 'rings'), which gives pair-specific instructional coherence beyond generic repetition or mere shared hierarchy. However, the endpoints sit in different Skill Areas and Sub-strands and target different capabilities, and the linking evidence is thin (one shared LC tag token 'movement', jaccard 0.125; text-token overlap limited to 'and'/'to'; weak same-rank proximity). Same-rank development would require substantive evidence of extended capability, which is not present - the differing scope makes the absence of a '(with help)' qualifier in the Term 2 statement an unreliable indicator of increased independence. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment, with null direction. Both endpoints have truncated source evidence and upstream audit/merge context, which limits confidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 3 Shared Reading (Reading and Phonics) Skills dealing with graphical texts, but at different terms within the same grade. The second SFI sits under Grade 3 / TERM 1 ('Uses visual cues to talk about a graphical text, e.g., looks at a photograph, and discusses what it is about, where it was taken'), an oral, cue-based engagement with a single picture. The first SFI sits under Grade 3 / TERM 3 ('Interprets information from graphical texts such as advertisements, pictures, graphs, charts'), extending from talking about visual cues to interpreting information across a wider and more abstract range of graphical text types (advertisements, graphs, charts). Learning Component tags corroborate the shared 'graphical text'/reading focus while showing the shift from 'visual cues/discussion' to 'interpreting information'. Earlier-term proficiency in reading visual cues plausibly supports the later-term interpretive demand, so buildsTowards runs Term 1 (second) to Term 3 (first), the permitted within-grade earlier-to-later direction. Note both endpoints' source evidence excerpts are truncated (24 omitted items each), so judgment rests on the bounded statement text, identity scope and hierarchy supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both SFIs are Grade 3 WRITING > 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' Skills: the first is Term 4 'Uses phonics knowledge and spelling rules to write more difficult words' (LC tags phonics, spelling, words, writing), the second is Term 2 'Reads and edits own writing by correcting spelling, punctuation, etc.' (LCs 'Reads own writing' and 'Edits own writing by correcting spelling, punctuation, etc.'). They share substantive coherence around spelling accuracy in learners' own writing, but they are distinct capabilities (generative encoding of harder words via phonics/spelling rules versus the revision/self-editing step of the writing process), and the evidence does not show one as a developmental extension of the other. Direction is also constrained: within Grade 3 a buildsTowards may only run from the earlier Term 2 statement to the later Term 4 statement, and the editing/proofreading skill is not shown to be what enables application of spelling rules to more difficult words (if anything the encoding knowledge supports the editing, a direction not permitted here). Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment. Note both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all ancestors carry upstream merge/audit context, so the bounded excerpts may not show the full term-level statements.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit under the same Grade 2 (rank 2), Term 3, Reading and Phonics / 'Daily Phonic Activities of 15 minutes:' sub-strand on page 97, so hierarchy alone is not decisive; the judgment rests on statement content. The first SFI is aural/phonological recognition of the onset and rime in complex blend patterns ('dr-eam, cr-eam, scr-eam, str-eam'; LC tags onset, rime, phonics), while the second requires actively using consonant blends to build up and break down words (LCs 'Uses consonant blends to build up words' and 'to break down words'). Recognising a blended onset separated from its rime is the recognition-level capability that supports the more demanding productive segmenting/blending of words with consonant blends, so proficiency in the first supports success in the second. Same-Term placement is permitted for buildsTowards within a grade (earlier-or-same Term), and the direction is grounded in the recognition-to-manipulation shift rather than repeated wording (token overlap is only 'and'). Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all endpoints/ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, so this inference is based on the bounded excerpts supplied.

judgment.rationale: First SFI (Grade 1, Term 4, Listening and Speaking (Oral), 'Twice weekly focussed listening and speaking activities') is an oral skill: 'Tells a familiar story which has a beginning, middle and end, varying tone and volume of voice', with LCs on story structure and vocal expression. Second SFI (Grade 1, Term 2, Reading and Phonics, 'Paired/Independent Reading') is 'Rereads familiar texts such as those read in Shared Reading sessions', an LC tagged rereading/shared reading/familiar texts. Both are Grade 1 (rank 1), and the Term 2 to Term 4 order would permit a second_to_first developmental claim, but the evidence does not show that rereading practice is a capability on which oral narrative retelling with structure and vocal variation depends; the overlap in the supplied evidence is essentially the single token 'familiar' plus the shared Grade banner. There is, however, genuine conceptual coherence: repeated encounters with familiar shared-reading stories and oral retelling of familiar stories are complementary narrative-literacy experiences across the Oral and Reading skill areas, so a symmetric relatesTo is the best-supported judgment rather than a dependency claim. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all endpoints/ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, so a stronger developmental reading cannot be confirmed from this bounded excerpt.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Grade R (resolved coordinate, rank 0) Skill statements in the emergent-literacy programme: the first is Term 3, Skill Area 'Emergent Reading', Sub-strand 'Emergent reading skills' — 'Develops directionality: ‘reads’ a series of pictures or arrows from left to right and top to bottom'; the second is Term 4, Skill Area 'Emergent Writing', Sub-strand 'Works with words' — 'Identifies a letter or a space between words in print such as their names or familiar words or in a book'. They share substantive conceptual coherence as complementary concepts-about-print capabilities: how text is traversed (left-to-right, top-to-bottom sequencing) and how print is segmented into units (letters, spaces between words in names, familiar words and books). Working on either meaningfully reinforces the learner's understanding of print organisation, so this is more than similar wording or shared hierarchy. buildsTowards is not adopted: although Term 3 → Term 4 within Grade R would be a permissible direction, the second statement is not an extension, deepening, combination or increased-complexity form of the first — it addresses a different capability (unit discrimination in actual print) in a different Skill Area, and nothing in the bounded evidence shows the later skill incorporating or presupposing directionality. The nomination signals are weak and non-semantic (shared Grade ancestor at distance 4 for both, rank_gap 0 flagged 'weak', token overlaps limited to 'a'/'or' and the tag token 'emergent'), and were not treated as progression evidence. Limitations: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and the second endpoint's supporting LC metadata is truncated, and that LC is shared by three sibling SFIs reflecting CAPS repetition of the bullet; all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, which is retained in the warnings and does not resolve into additional semantic evidence.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit under the same Grade R / Term 4 / Emergent Writing / Emergent Handwriting sub-strand (same page 56 table row 4), so neither has a rank or term advantage over the other. 'Form letters with their bodies in pairs or on their own' is a whole-body letter-shape activity (LC tags: emergent writing, handwriting, letter formation), while 'Plays finger rhymes with finger actions' is a fine-motor/finger-action activity (LC tags: emergent handwriting, fine motor, finger rhymes). They are complementary pre-handwriting readiness activities within one sub-strand: substantive coherence in preparing for letter writing, but the evidence does not show that proficiency in either is developmentally required for or materially predictive of the other (gross-motor letter shaping vs finger dexterity are parallel strands listed side by side in the same term). The only lexical overlap is the stopword 'with', and shared ancestors/page proximity alone cannot establish direction. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so no further distinguishing detail is available; symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment.

Proficiency with vowel digraphs is not shown to support the consonant-digraph revision (which looks back to earlier teaching rather than forward from the Term 2 bullet), so this is complementary, mutually reinforcing phonics knowledge rather than a developmental dependency. judgment.rationale: Both are Grade 1 Reading and Phonics (Phonics sub-strand) Skills about building up and breaking down words. The first (Grade 1, Term 2, per identity scope grade=grade 1|term=term 2) is limited to simple words beginning with a single consonant, segmented into onset and rime (h-en, p-en), with LCs for blending, segmenting and rhyme identification. The second (Grade 1, Term 4) extends the same build-up/break-down operation to words with consonant blends as onsets (sp-o-t, fr-o-g, dr-i-nk, st-i-ck), a substantive increase in phonological complexity rather than repeated wording alone. Within Grade 1 the direction runs from the earlier Term 2 statement to the later Term 4 statement, so proficiency in single-consonant onset-rime blending/segmenting supports success with consonant-blend word building. Both endpoints' source evidence excerpts are truncated and ancestors carry merge context, but the printed statement text and term scoping are unambiguous.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Grade R, Term 3 Skills (identical rank 0 and the same Term node), but they sit in different Skill Areas: the first is Emergent Reading / 'Emergent reading skills' ('‘Reads’ picture books with three or four predictable sentences'), the second is Emergent Writing / 'Emergent Writing:' ('Role plays writing in play situations... ‘writes’ lists'). Their substantive coherence is the reciprocal emergent-literacy approximation behaviour: pretend 'reading' of simple predictable text and pretend 'writing' in play both build print awareness and the understanding that print carries meaning, so they meaningfully reinforce one another within the same term. The evidence shows no expanded capability, dependency or sequencing of one on the other (same grade and same term, distinct strands, LC overlap limited to the generic token 'emergent' and the phrase 'for example'), so no developmental direction is asserted. Note that both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each) and all endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context; this limits but does not contradict the reading above.

judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade 3 (rank 3), Term 4, Skill Area 'Reading and Phonics', but under different sub-strands: Shared Reading ('Uses visual cues to read graphical texts and starts to analyse text for attitudes and assumptions') and Group Guided Reading ('Reads both silently and out loud from own book in a guided reading group... at the instructional level of the group'). They are complementary components of the same term's reading programme - teacher-led critical/visual text interpretation alongside levelled guided oral and silent reading practice - so there is substantive conceptual coherence in reading development. However, neither statement extends, deepens, or presupposes the other: analysing advertisements for attitudes is not a stated expansion of guided-group decoding/fluency, and vice versa, and both are same-grade, same-term, giving no rank or term-order basis for a developmental direction. Evidence overlap is mainly generic ('reading', 'and', shared ancestors, same source page), which alone cannot establish dependency. Noted limitation: source evidence for both endpoints is truncated and LC evidence for 91a8b218 is truncated, so finer-grained dependency evidence may exist but is not available here.

judgment.rationale: Both are Grade R (rank 0) Emergent Reading Skills, but the source-backed identity scopes differ by term: the first is Grade R Term 1 ('Recognises own name and names of at least five other children in the class', sub-strand 'Emergent reading skills'), the second is Grade R Term 2 ('Understands that print communicates meaning. Knows words can represent own name, names of people, places and things', sub-strand 'Emergent reading'). Direction Term 1 to Term 2 is permitted within the grade. This is not mere repeated wording: the Term 1 skill is concrete recognition of a small set of specific written names, while the Term 2 skill generalises that experience into the print-awareness concepts that print carries meaning and that words can stand for names of people, places and things (LCs 'Understands that print communicates meaning' and 'Knows words can represent own name, names of people, places and things'). Reliably recognising one's own and classmates' written names supports success with that broader generalisation, so proficiency in the first supports the second.
